summary: Describes using the Stac LZS data compression algorithm, with one or several compression histories, to compress PPP packets. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: One company's way to shrink data on a PPP link so it travels faster.

what is a ppp compression history
subtitle: How PPP compresses packets with Stac LZS, using one or many histories and CCP resets to stay in sync.

tldr.problem: Compressing PPP packets with a running history saves bandwidth, but any lost, damaged or reordered packet leaves the two ends out of sync.
tldr.mechanism: Each packet carries one Stac LZS compressed datagram, optionally with a history number and a check value (LCB, CRC or sequence number). A receiver that detects a failure sends a CCP Reset-Request and the sender clears that history and answers with a Reset-Ack.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational specification of the CCP Stac LZS option (type 17). It also defines an optional Extended Mode that signals resets with a flag bit and a 12-bit coherency count instead of Reset-Ack.

today: RFC 1974 is an Informational RFC and the data shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. A later enhanced variant of the protocol using a Data Compression Protocol header is described in RFC 1967.

sections.title: Stac LZS and Compression Histories
sections.content:
Stac LZS is a compression algorithm from Stac Electronics, starting from a sliding window compression history similar to LZ1. The RFC says it is optimized to compress all file types efficiently, and even string matches as short as two octets are effectively compressed.

It supports a single history or multiple histories. A single history needs the least memory but may compress less. When several independent streams share a link, giving each its own history can improve the compression ratio.
sections.plainLanguage: Squeezing works best when you remember what you already sent. You can keep one notebook or one per conversation.

sections.title: Carrying LZS in PPP
sections.content:
Once PPP reaches the Network-Layer Protocol phase and CCP is Opened with LZS as the primary algorithm, one Stac LZS datagram goes in the PPP Information field, with Protocol 00FD or, for compression on individual links, 00FB. If CCP is not Opened or LZS is not primary, the Protocol field is 4021 (Stac LZS) and the default format applies: one history, no history number, no check value. LCP Protocol-Reject ends that use.

LCP and NCP packets MUST NOT be sent inside LZS packets. The compressed block always ends with an end marker, so trailing bits and octets can be treated as padding. If the sender adds no padding, trailing zero octets MAY be removed and one MUST be appended on receipt.

The maximum expansion is 12.5%. If expansion would exceed the peer's MRU, the packet MUST be sent uncompressed with its native PPP Protocol ID and the history reset. If most packets expand, for example because the data is already compressed, the transmitter SHOULD stop compressing and may resume later.
sections.plainLanguage: Squeezed packets get a special label. If squeezing would make a packet bigger, it goes out plain and the notebook is wiped.

sections.title: Packet Format and Check Values
sections.content:
The packet is the PPP Protocol field, an optional History Number, an optional Check Value, then the compressed data. The history number is absent when the History Count is below 2, one octet for 2 to 255, and two octets for 256 or more. The check value is 0, 1 or 2 octets; by default a one-octet sequence number is used.

  • LCB: one octet, the exclusive-OR of FF hex and each octet of the uncompressed datagram.
  • CRC: two octets, initialized to FFFF hex per packet and based on the HDLC FCS-16 polynomial; the ones complement is sent least significant octet first.
  • Sequence number: one octet, starting at 1 and incrementing modulo 256 per history.

The data field holds exactly one datagram in compressed form as defined in section 3.2 of ANSI X3.241-1994.
sections.plainLanguage: Each squeezed packet can carry a small check number, like a page number or a tally, so the receiver can tell if something is missing or scrambled.

sections.title: Staying in Sync with Reset-Request and Reset-Ack
sections.content:
With one or more histories, an implementation MUST either use a reliable lower-layer link protocol, keep the histories synchronized, or both. To synchronize it MUST use the CCP Reset-Request (Code 14) and Reset-Ack (Code 15) messages and MUST support the sequence number check mode. Their Data field holds the two-octet History Number, most significant octet first (1 when no history number is present).

When the receiver sees a sequence mismatch or a bad LCB or CRC, it MUST send a Reset-Request, silently discard compressed packets for that history, and keep doing so until a Reset-Ack with the matching Identifier arrives. The transmitter MUST reset the affected history and reply with a Reset-Ack that copies the Identifier and history number. The sequence number is not reset. The RFC walks through an example where packets 103 and 106 are lost and the receiver repeats its request.

If neither a reliable link nor these mechanisms exist, histories MUST be reset after every datagram. The RFC notes a decompressor cannot recover from dropped, erroneous or misordered datagrams and propagates errors until both peers reset.
sections.plainLanguage: When a receiver notices a gap, it shouts 'start over', ignores everything until the sender says 'okay, restarted', and then goes on as normal.

sections.title: The Configuration Option
sections.content:
The CCP Stac LZS option has Type 17, Length 5, a two-octet History Count and a Check Mode. History Count 0 means the peer clears the history before every packet, 1 is the default and 2 to 65535 allow several histories; the sender need not use as many as the receiver accepts, but each peer allocates resources for the negotiated number.

Check Mode is bit-mapped; the three low bits hold one of five values and the upper five bits are reserved and set to 0. Sequence Numbers MUST be implemented for compatibility; the other modes MAY be.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends agree up front on how many notebooks to keep and which kind of mistake check to use.

sections.title: Extended Mode
sections.content:
Check Mode 4 selects Extended Mode, which supports only a history count of 1 and changes the packet format. After the PPP Protocol field (00FD, with protocol-field compression forbidden) come four flag bits A to D and a 12-bit coherency count. Bit A is PACKET_FLUSHED (the history was just reset, so the packet can always be decompressed), Bit C is PACKET_COMPRESSED, and B and D are unused with Stac LZS.

The coherency count starts at 0, rises by 1 for each PPP packet sent, and wraps after all bits are 1. On a bad count or a corrupt packet the decompressor drops it and sends a CCP Reset-Request. The compressor clears its history and sets PACKET_FLUSHED on its next frame, and the decompressor adopts the new count. The RFC concludes that synchronization needs no Reset-Ack.
sections.plainLanguage: In this mode the sender just raises a 'fresh start' flag on its next packet, so nobody has to send an extra confirmation.
